strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: learning from rich, serialized natural-language trajectories (execution traces plus evaluation traces) rather than sparse scalar rewards is a compelling and well-argued hypothesis, and the paper operationalizes it concretely.

Technically well-specified method: the genetic optimization loop, reflective prompt mutation, and instance-wise Pareto-based candidate selection are clearly formalized (Algorithms 1-2), with the Pareto 'illumination' design well-motivated by the local-optima failure mode.

Strong and broad empirical evaluation: four diverse benchmarks (HotpotQA, IFBench, HoVer, PUPA), two model families (Qwen3 8B, GPT-4.1 mini), comparisons against both a weight-space RL baseline (GRPO with LoRA, 24k rollouts) and the leading prompt optimizer (MIPROv2), with rollout budgets aligned across methods (within ~10%).
Useful ablation: the SelectBestCandidate vs. Pareto-based sampling ablation (Table 2, Figure 6) directly validates the central design choice and provides instructive search-tree visualizations.
Sample-efficiency claims are supported by detailed rollout accounting, including the honest observation that most of GEPA's rollouts go to validation and the more favorable train-only rollout counts.

Additional practical analyses (generalization gap, prompt length/cost analysis up to 9.2x shorter prompts) and promising preliminary inference-time search results on NPUEval/KernelBench broaden the contribution's applicability.

Transparency and reproducibility support: meta-prompts, intermediate prompts, full search trees, and per-benchmark rollout counts are provided in the appendix; limitations are candidly discussed (Section 8), including when weight updates may outperform prompting.
weaknesses: Fairness of the GRPO comparison is debatable: GEPA exploits a custom textual feedback function µ_f (e.g., per-hop document feedback, constraint descriptions) that GRPO does not receive; this asymmetric information access makes 'prompt evolution beats RL' claims harder to attribute purely to the learning medium. No RL baseline with richer textual reward shaping is provided.

Only LoRA-based GRPO is evaluated; full-parameter RL fine-tuning is acknowledged but not attempted, and hyperparameter exploration for GRPO appears limited ('manually explore several values'). The headline claim of outperforming RL rests on one possibly under-tuned baseline.

No variance reporting: results appear to be single runs per (benchmark, model, optimizer) configuration; with small test sets (e.g., 221-300 examples, 294 for IFBench), differences of a few points may not be statistically significant. Multiple seeds with error bars or significance tests are needed.

GEPA+Merge behaves inconsistently (degrades Qwen3 8B on most tasks, improves GPT-4.1 mini), and the paper attributes this to budget allocation/timing hyperparameters chosen suboptimally, which weakens the method's robustness claim; the merge strategy lacks systematic study.

The inference-time search experiments (Section 6) are preliminary and lack baselines from comparable evolutionary search methods (e.g., OpenEvolve-style code search) or prompt-optimization alternatives, so their significance is unclear.

Scaling and generalization remain open: only two LLMs, small training sets (~150 examples), and benchmarks largely sourced from one prior work (Tan et al., 2025); whether the approach holds for frontier-scale models, larger action spaces, or non-textual/latent-state systems is untested.

The feedback-engineering burden (designing µ_f per task) is a real adoption cost that is acknowledged but not quantified; how much of the gain comes from well-designed task-specific feedback versus the optimizer itself is not isolated (e.g., an ablation of GEPA with generic 'success/failure' feedback is missing).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: adapting compound AI systems under a limited rollout budget is an important practical problem, and the formulation in Section 2 (optimizing under a hard rollout constraint) is crisp.

GEPA is a sensible combination of known ideas (evolutionary prompt mutation, Pareto/illumination-based candidate selection, LLM reflection) assembled into a coherent optimizer, and the algorithm is described in enough detail (Algorithms 1-4, meta-prompt in Appendix B) to be reproducible in principle.

Results are strong on their face: consistent improvements over MIPROv2 across four benchmarks and two models, with budget matched on a per-benchmark basis, plus a meaningful ablation (SelectBestCandidate vs. Pareto sampling) supporting one of the core design choices.

Useful supporting analyses: generalization-gap comparison following Wan et al. (2024), prompt-length/cost analysis, and qualitative visualization of search trees that illustrate why greedy selection stalls.
Honest limitations section acknowledging that weight-space RL may win in data-rich regimes and that feedback engineering is underexplored.
weaknesses: The headline claim ('can outperform reinforcement learning') rests on a narrow and arguably uneven comparison: GRPO is run only on Qwen3 8B with LoRA, at 24k rollouts, on 4 tasks. No full-parameter RL baseline, no tuning-matched RL baseline, and no other RL method (e.g., PPO variants) are evaluated. RL is a moving target and the title overstates the scope of the evidence.

A confound undermines the GRPO comparison: GEPA consumes rich, hand-engineered textual feedback (module-level retrieval hints, constraint descriptions, PAPILLON score breakdowns), while GRPO receives only scalar rewards. The gains may substantially reflect the information asymmetry in the feedback channels rather than 'learning in natural language.' An RL baseline with denser/verifier-style rewards, or a GEPA ablation without the engineered feedback function, is needed to attribute the improvement to the claimed mechanism.

Evaluation is thin statistically: four benchmarks with small test sets (150-300 examples), apparently single optimization runs per configuration, no error bars, seeds, or significance tests. Several reported margins (e.g., IFBench +2.7% over GRPO, or GEPA vs. GEPA+Merge differences) could plausibly be noise at these sample sizes.

Benchmarks are borrowed wholesale from one prior benchmark suite (Tan et al., 2025) with small modified splits; the tasks are QA/retrieval-centric, limiting evidence for the breadth of 'compound AI systems' the formulation claims to cover (no agentic/tool-use tasks with long horizons in the main comparison).

Novelty is incremental: the core loop is prompt evolution with LLM-proposed mutations (EvoPrompt, Promptbreeder, OPRO, TextGrad) combined with MAP-Elites-style illumination (Mouret & Clune, 2015). The Pareto selection and Merge components are reasonable engineering but not a fundamentally new learning principle; the paper's contribution is more empirical than conceptual.

GEPA+Merge behaves inconsistently (helps GPT-4.1 mini, degrades Qwen3 8B on 3 of 4 tasks), and the explanation is post-hoc with hyperparameters admittedly left fixed; this weakens the story that the method is robust across models.

The inference-time search experiments (NPUEval, KernelBench) are preliminary: no budget-matched baseline comparisons on KernelBench, and results are explicitly acknowledged as early, so they add little evidentiary weight.

Presentation issues: several typos ('countts', 'satsified', 'leanring', 'evidences by'), dense and hard-to-parse composite figures (Figure 3), and a Figure 16 caption that does not match its content (prompt sizes, not test performance). Minor, but they suggest the paper was not carefully polished.

Claims about sample efficiency partially double-count: the 35x/78x efficiency numbers count rollouts, but GEPA's rollouts include full validation-set evaluations for candidate selection; the train-only rollout counts given later are more honest, yet the abstract and Figure 1 emphasize the larger numbers.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: exploiting the natural-language traces of compound AI systems as a richer learning signal than scalar RL rewards, and operationalizing it as reflective prompt evolution with Pareto-based candidate selection.

Comprehensive evaluation across four diverse tasks (multi-hop QA, instruction following, privacy-preserving delegation, claim verification), two models spanning open (Qwen3 8B) and proprietary (GPT-4.1 mini) families, with careful budget-matching against both a strong prompt optimizer (MIPROv2) and an RL baseline (GRPO with LoRA).

Convincing headline results: GEPA outperforms GRPO by ~10% on average with up to 35x fewer rollouts and beats MIPROv2 on every benchmark/model, more than doubling the aggregate optimization gains (+14% vs +7%).

Useful ablations: the SelectBestCandidate ablation (Table 2) isolates the contribution of Pareto-based candidate selection (+6.4% aggregate), and analysis of prompt length (up to 9.2x shorter than MIPROv2) and generalization gaps (Figure 14) add practical insight beyond raw scores.

Strong qualitative and mechanistic analysis: optimization trajectory visualizations (Figures 5-6, search trees in the appendix), full-length evolved prompts, and the meta-prompt are released, aiding interpretability and reproducibility.

The 'feedback function' (mu_f) idea of exposing evaluation traces (e.g., compiler errors) as diagnostic signal is a valuable, generalizable contribution, demonstrated in promising preliminary inference-time search experiments (NPUEval, KernelBench).

Honest limitations section acknowledging that weight-space learning may win when rollouts are cheap, that Merge hyperparameters are suboptimal, and that most rollouts are spent on validation rather than learning.
weaknesses: The GRPO baseline is limited: LoRA-only finetuning (rank 16) at 8B scale with only 'manual' hyperparameter exploration; no full-parameter finetuning or stronger RL variants (e.g., with more careful reward shaping), so the headline 'can outperform reinforcement learning' claim rests on a comparatively weak configuration of the competitor.

Results appear to be single-run per configuration; no error bars, confidence intervals, or variance over seeds are reported, which is concerning given the stochastic nature of both optimization and LLM evaluation on small test sets (e.g., 58-300 test examples).

Feedback functions are hand-engineered per benchmark (e.g., module-level hop feedback, constraint satisfaction breakdowns); this provides a significant, task-specific information advantage over baselines that do not receive such feedback, raising questions about how much of the gain comes from the algorithm versus this richer supervision.

Only four benchmarks, mostly drawn from a single prior benchmark suite (Tan et al. 2025); generality to larger training sets, multi-model pipelines, or systems with heterogeneous modules remains untested.

GEPA+Merge results are inconsistent (worse than GEPA on Qwen3 8B overall), and the explanation for this is post-hoc; the merge component feels under-developed relative to its inclusion in the title system.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence (e.g., 'can outperform RL' in the title generalizes from one RL algorithm at one model scale), and the inference-time search results are explicitly preliminary without baselines matched in budget.

Pareto-set computation and full-validation evaluation per accepted candidate means substantial inference cost in practice; the sample-efficiency framing conflates train rollouts (small) with total rollouts (large), which could be made clearer throughout.

strengths: The central idea is well-motivated and clearly articulated: serialized LLM system trajectories are a richer learning medium than scalar rewards, and GEPA operationalizes this via reflective mutation plus Pareto-based candidate selection, which is a meaningful and practical contribution to prompt optimization for compound AI systems.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across six diverse benchmarks (multi-hop QA, math, instruction following, privacy delegation, retrieval verification), two model families (open Qwen3-8B and closed GPT-4.1 Mini), and multiple strong baselines (GRPO, MIPROv2, TextGrad, Trace/OptoPrime), with results favoring GEPA on most settings.

The sample-efficiency claims are carefully analyzed: the paper distinguishes train vs. validation rollout accounting, reports rollout counts per benchmark, includes a full-parameter GRPO finetuning comparison (Fig. 11), and discusses that most of GEPA's budget goes to candidate selection rather than learning signal.

Good ablations: Pareto-based candidate selection is compared against greedy (SelectBestCandidate) and BeamSearch variants under the same evolution harness (Table 3, Fig. 6), isolating the contribution of the Pareto strategy; the Merge crossover is studied with honest reporting of where it fails (Qwen3 8B degradation).

Valuable additional analyses: prompt length/cost comparisons, cross-model transfer of optimized prompts (GEPA-Qwen-Opt on GPT-4.1 Mini), generalization-gap analysis following Wan et al. (2024), and qualitative prompt evolution trees that provide insight into how the optimizer accumulates strategies.
Extensive appendices (meta-prompts, full optimized prompts, hyperparameters, costs, search trees) substantially support reproducibility, and code is released.
Extended applications (inference-time kernel code optimization on NPUEval/KernelBench, adversarial prompt search) demonstrate the flexibility of the framework beyond standard prompt tuning.
weaknesses: Comparisons to GRPO involve different parameter spaces (weight updates vs. prompt updates) and different assumptions; GRPO learns generalizable weights while GEPA produces task-specific prompts, so 'outperforms RL' claims should be interpreted within the fixed-weight compound-AI setting, and generalization to truly novel task distributions is not fully explored for either method.

GEPA leverages rich per-module textual feedback functions (µf) that were hand-crafted per benchmark; although Trace/TextGrad are given the same metric/feedback, Trace does not support per-module feedback, so a portion of GEPA's advantage may stem from feedback design rather than the evolutionary search itself. No ablation quantifies GEPA's performance when restricted to the same global-feedback interface.

Statistical rigor is limited: no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed variance are reported for the main tables, and several test sets are small (e.g., 30 AIME problems, 58 IFBench constraints), making single-run gains (often of a few points) hard to assess for significance.

Some headline numbers are inconsistent or partially undercut within the paper: e.g., GEPA+Merge degrades IFBench on Qwen3-8B (28.23 vs. baseline 36.90) yet the abstract emphasizes 'up to' gains; GRPO wins on AIME-2025, and Merge's benefit appears model-dependent without a principled selection rule.

The claim that instruction-only optimization now beats joint instruction+few-shot optimization rests on only six tasks and two models; the 'shift in trend' narrative (contradicting Wan et al. 2024) would benefit from broader task coverage and closer control of prompt-length budgets for MIPROv2.

Adversarial prompt search and inference-time code search results are presented as promising but preliminary; the NPUEval comparison mixes ablations (Sequential10, RAG, MIPROv2) with different budgets/agents, weakening those conclusions.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important question: whether natural-language reflection over trajectories is a more sample-efficient adaptation medium than weight-space RL (GRPO) for compound AI systems. The core idea—merging reflective prompt mutation with Pareto-frontier candidate selection—is clearly motivated and reasonably novel relative to prior prompt optimizers (MIPROv2, TextGrad, APO, Promptbreeder).

The algorithm is well formalized (Algorithms 1–4), with a full description of the genetic loop, feedback functions, Pareto-based selection, and the system-aware merge crossover, enabling reproduction.

Evaluation breadth is above average for this area: six benchmarks (HotpotQA, IFBench, HoVer, PUPA, AIME-2025, LiveBench-Math), two model families (Qwen3 8B and GPT-4.1 Mini), multiple baselines (MIPROv2, Trace/OptoPrime, TextGrad, GRPO with LoRA and full finetuning), matched rollout budgets against MIPROv2, and a selection-strategy ablation (SelectBestCandidate vs. BeamSearch vs. Pareto) that isolates the contribution of the Pareto sampling.

Several analyses add credibility: generalization gap study following Wan et al. (2024), cross-model transfer of Qwen-optimized prompts to GPT-4.1-Mini, prompt-length/cost analysis, rollout-budget accounting for the train-only sample-efficiency claims, and explicit monetary costs of experiments.
Honest limitations are acknowledged (e.g., GEPA+Merge underperforming on Qwen3 8B, hyperparameter sensitivity of merge invocation, extended applications labeled as preliminary), and code is released.
weaknesses: The headline claim 'reflective prompt evolution can outperform reinforcement learning' is stronger than the evidence. The comparison is against GRPO only, on a limited set of (mostly small) compound AI systems, with a single LoRA/full-FT configuration and manually explored hyperparameters. No stronger RL baselines (e.g., tuned PPO variants, multi-module GRPO variants beyond one implementation) or test-time scaling baselines are included, so a general claim about RL vs. language-space learning is not established.

Statistical rigor is weak: results appear to be single runs with no seeds, confidence intervals, or variance reporting across stochastic optimization. Given GEPA's highly stochastic search (stochastic candidate sampling, minibatch evaluation, reflection LLM calls), run-to-run variance could materially affect the reported margins on several benchmarks (e.g., IFBench differences of <1 point on Qwen3 8B).

The sample-efficiency claims ('up to 35x fewer rollouts', '78x greater sample efficiency') depend on an accounting choice: most of GEPA's budget is spent on validation rollouts used for candidate selection, and the paper itself concedes that on train-only rollouts the numbers are far smaller. The narrative leads with the more flattering number.

Potential prompt-overfitting confound: GEPA-optimized prompts include very task-specific declarative rules and even literal examples from training feedback (e.g., 'Madeira archipelago population in 2011', specific HotpotQA answers embedded in the final-answer prompt). This raises questions about contamination-style memorization from the feedback/minibatch data and whether gains will transfer to distribution shift; the generalization gap analysis partially addresses this but only on three benchmarks.

GEPA+Merge is inconsistent (degrades Qwen3 8B aggregate vs. GEPA), and merge hyperparameters are admitted to be suboptimal; this weakens the paper's best-reported numbers (+13.33%) as a general configuration.

GRPO is evaluated with 24,000 rollouts under settings that may not be tuned for multi-module compound systems; the fairness of comparing a weight-update method constrained to these configurations against a prompt search that also consumes the validation set for selection deserves more scrutiny.

Extended applications (NPUEval, KernelBench, adversarial prompt search) are interesting but preliminary, single-config, and lack baselines (e.g., OpenEvolve/AlphaEvolve-style baselines for the code tasks), so they contribute anecdotes rather than evidence.

strengths: Clear and timely problem framing: sample-efficiency of prompt-space adaptation versus RL, with a well-motivated thesis that natural-language traces provide richer learning signal than scalar rewards.

GEPA is a well-specified, principled method combining reflective mutation, evaluation traces as feedback, Pareto-based candidate selection, and a system-aware crossover (Merge), with full algorithms provided and code released.

Broad and fairly rigorous empirical evaluation: six diverse benchmarks, two model families (open Qwen3 8B and GPT-4.1 Mini), strong baselines (GRPO with LoRA and full finetuning, MIPROv2, TextGrad, Trace), matched rollout budgets with reported discrepancies (~10%), and detailed appendix on experimental setup and costs.
The Pareto-selection ablation (vs. greedy and beam-search selection) is a genuinely informative study isolating a key design choice, backed by search-tree visualizations.

Notable secondary findings: instruction-only prompts beating joint instruction+demonstration optimization, cross-model transfer of GEPA prompts, shorter prompts with lower generalization gap, and promising inference-time search and adversarial prompt-search applications.

Practical significance: low monetary cost, works on closed-source models, released code and full optimized prompts make the work highly reproducible and impactful for practitioners building compound AI systems.
weaknesses: Results appear to come from single optimization runs without error bars, confidence intervals, or variance across seeds; given stochastic search and small test sets (e.g., AIME-2025 with 30 questions), some margins may not be statistically significant.

The headline claim 'outperforms RL' is somewhat overbroad: it rests on one model (Qwen3 8B), compound/single-module pipelines, and GRPO with 24k rollouts; on AIME GEPA actually trails GRPO, and the comparison conflates different hypothesis spaces (weights vs. prompts) without acknowledging cases where RL remains necessary.

Fairness of the sample-efficiency accounting is debatable: the majority of GEPA's rollout budget is spent on validation for candidate selection, and the '35x fewer rollouts' comparisons depend on budget-allocation choices; the authors themselves note smaller validation subsets as future work.

GEPA relies on rich, task-specific feedback functions (mu_f) and hand-designed text feedback; this requirement is a real limitation versus scalar-reward RL, and the paper could more prominently discuss when such feedback is unavailable.
GEPA+Merge results are inconsistent across models (degrading Qwen3 8B aggregates), and the explanation (hyperparameter choices) is acknowledged as unresolved, leaving a methodological loose end.

Some analyses (e.g., prompt-length advantage, cross-model transfer) are on a small number of tasks and would benefit from more tasks or models; the inference-time code-search experiments are explicitly preliminary.
